title: Household-scale markets for national, occupational, and housing income risk

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a set of durable, affordable markets through which households could insure the parts of their future income and housing wealth that move with a country, occupation or local housing market. Contracts would link payments to a shared income or price index. A household exposed to a decline in that index could hold a position that pays when the decline occurs, transferring some of its exposure to investors willing to bear it. Households could participate directly or through pension providers, mortgage providers or other intermediaries. This describes the intended capability, not an established household insurance system.

The defining advance would be the combination of usable contracts, sustained trading, trusted settlement and effective household hedging over long horizons. Merely creating an index or listing a derivative would establish only part of that capability. National and occupational contracts would address shared income shocks; local housing contracts would address movements in a housing index. None would automatically cover every individual's earnings loss or every property's change in value. This scope is a synthesis of the proposed market design.

significance.text: The economic motivation is the difficulty of insuring future labor income. According to the supplied review, Kocherlakota's March 1996 review documents both the difficulty of directly insuring labor-income fluctuations and enforcement and adverse-selection problems that prevent people from fully capitalizing future earnings. These historical findings explain why access to ordinary borrowing and investment need not give households comprehensive protection against income shocks. They do not establish a current ranking of households' largest risks or show that existing stocks and bonds are uniformly ineffective hedges.

Conditional impact assessment: effective, widely accessible markets could expand households' ability to insure lifetime resources. Their direct benefit would be lower exposure to the particular national, occupational or housing shocks covered by the contracts, after costs and losses from imperfect matching. The scale of that benefit would depend on participation, hedge effectiveness and counterparty performance. A material reduction in total lifetime-income variance would require measurement; it does not follow simply from a contract's availability.

The comparison with producers' use of commodity futures is a useful analogy for the proposed ability to transfer a shared economic exposure. Its limits matter: household exposures can last decades, vary substantially between individuals and be difficult to finance against. An index hedge can leave substantial basis risk—the difference between the index movement and the household's actual loss. Conditional downstream possibilities include less pressure to concentrate savings in assets tied to one's own locality or economy and greater ability to withstand occupational decline. These are proposed benefits, not demonstrated consequences.

Broader international effects are possible but would not be necessary evidence of success. The supplied Wikipedia review confirms that the Backus–Kehoe–Kydland consumption-correlation puzzle concerns consumption being less correlated across countries than output, while the equity-home-bias puzzle concerns limited foreign-equity holdings. Successful household hedging could coexist with both patterns: participation might be limited, and people could share risk through income contracts while retaining domestically concentrated equity portfolios. These remain distinct empirical questions.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unsolved capability is an institution that turns a household's long-horizon exposure into a practical hedge whose insurance benefit exceeds its full cost. This requires more than financial engineering at issuance: households need access, counterparties willing to take the other side, credible enforcement and settlement, and continued liquidity when adverse shocks make insurance valuable. The supplied evidence does not establish how completely each component is missing in present-day markets.

Historical evidence supports an important financing obstacle. The reviewed 1996 Kocherlakota paper describes enforcement and adverse-selection constraints on borrowing against future labor income. A household can therefore possess valuable future earning capacity without being able to turn it into sufficient financing for an insurance position. The stronger wording attributed to Campbell's 2007 slides—that human capital cannot be collateralized—cannot be independently checked from the retained materials because those slides were not captured.

Proposed design barriers include balancing moral hazard against basis risk. A contract linked closely to an individual's earnings could create incentives or information problems around effort, reporting and eligibility. A broad index reduces dependence on individual behavior but may compensate poorly for that person's actual loss. National, occupational and local housing indices would each require choices about coverage, measurement, publication delays, revisions and settlement rules. These are concrete issues to resolve in designing the proposed markets; their relative importance is not established by the available source texts.

Financing and market formation are additional candidate barriers. Margin calls could demand cash from households during the same downturn the hedge is intended to protect against; counterparty default could impair promised payments; and thin trading could produce spreads that consume the insurance benefit. Sustained participation would require a workable allocation of financing burdens and enough investors willing to hold the opposite exposure. The research attributes startup-cost and contract-enforcement concerns to Athanasoulis, Shiller and van Wincoop's 1999 paper, but the source index contains no retained text with which to verify that attribution or its full argument.

current_state.text: The strongest retained historical evidence described in the supplied review is Kocherlakota's March 1996 review. Its identified, untruncated PDF documents incomplete insurance of labor income and constraints on capitalizing future earnings. That establishes an older economic motivation and a class of financing problems. It does not establish the current availability, affordability or effectiveness of national-income, occupational-income and local-housing hedges.

The research identifies Athanasoulis, Shiller and van Wincoop's April 1999 paper, Macro Markets and Financial Security, as an account of macro-market proposals and their barriers. It also cites Campbell's 19 June 2007 discussion slides for the household collateral constraint. Neither source has a retained artifact in the supplied index. Their dated attributions and reported passages therefore remain unverified within this record; missing source capture is not evidence that the publications or arguments are false.

The research attributes to Julien Acalin's April 2026 IMF working paper the findings that sovereign growth-indexed bonds have rarely been issued, that indexing 20 percent of debt produces only modest tail-risk reduction, and that a sustained premium of 100 basis points would offset most gains for many countries. The IMF text was not retained, so these numerical scenarios and conclusions cannot be verified here. Their interpretation also requires the model assumptions, the definition of tail risk and the treatment of the premium. Even if confirmed, sovereign debt stabilization would be a related application of growth-contingent finance, not a demonstration of household income insurance.

The research reports that CME listed metro-area Case–Shiller housing-index futures and that its delayed public quote page on 16 October 2026 showed volume of zero for the listed composite contract months. The page and snapshot were not retained, so neither the listing details nor the reported volumes can be verified from the supplied evidence. If the snapshot is accurate, it describes only those contracts at that observation time. It cannot establish a full trading history, sustained market inactivity, household participation or hedge effectiveness.

The research also reports that French growth-indexed bonds traded from 1956 to 1971 and that Panageas examined the episode in a May 2026 NBER paper. No corresponding source URL or reviewed text is supplied, so the episode's dates, contract features and paper attribution remain unverified here. If confirmed, this would be a historical example of growth-linked securities rather than evidence of a modern household-scale market.

The supplied review's bounded search record is empty, and the principal claimed 2026 materials lack retained artifacts. Consequently, this record cannot establish present-day market completeness or freshness as of 1 November 2026. The retained Wikipedia extraction was reported as complete and supports the descriptions and listing of the two international-economics puzzles. Its presence does not independently verify the proposed market mechanisms or the missing IMF, CME, SSRN and BIS evidence.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: contracts covering specified national-income, occupational-income or metropolitan housing exposures should sustain two-sided trading over a pre-specified multiyear period, with meaningful household participation directly or through identified intermediaries. Duration, participation, market depth, spreads and executable trade sizes should be defined before evaluation. These are proposed criteria for assessing the innovation, not established standards. Success in one contract family would demonstrate that scope rather than completion across all three.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained multiyear two-sided trading with meaningful household participation

completion_criteria.text: The central outcome should be a pre-registered minimum reduction in the relevant household risk, rather than merely a specified notional position or share of exposure traded. Evaluation should compare actual household or intermediary outcomes with an explicit unhedged benchmark, disclose remaining basis risk and separate protection of aggregate exposure from changes in total lifetime risk. Measured insurance benefits should exceed transaction, financing, margin, intermediation and settlement costs under a stated valuation method.
completion_criteria.label: Pre-registered minimum household risk reduction with benefits exceeding full costs

completion_criteria.text: A convincing demonstration should include stress-period performance: whether households can retain their hedges, meet cash demands and receive contractual payments during adverse shocks. Counterparty exposure, defaults, index revisions and exit costs should be reported. Reproducibility would require sufficiently documented contract terms, index construction, participation data and evaluation methods for independent analysts to assess the result, with any data-access restrictions made explicit.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible evidence of household hedge performance during adverse shocks

completion_criteria.text: Replication across different cohorts, occupations, places and economic conditions would establish demonstrated breadth. Finite tests cannot establish literal universality or eliminate individual effort-related risk. A one-time GDP warrant issued during a debt restructuring, or a listed future without sustained household hedging, would not satisfy this proposed demonstration. Such instruments could still supply useful evidence about individual components of the system.
completion_criteria.label: Replication establishes breadth across household groups and economic conditions

related_concepts.text: Synthesis from the supplied roster: ECO-01, Empirically valid aggregate market laws beyond the Sonnenschein–Mantel–Debreu barrier, could help describe the behavior of markets containing these contracts, but ECO-06 concerns building effective risk-sharing institutions rather than discovering general aggregate laws. ECO-09, A general, detail-free allocation compiler for private-information economies, overlaps with incentives and information problems in contract design; its general allocation objective is broader than providing these particular household hedges.

Synthesis from the supplied roster: ECO-02, Prospective transport of causal policy effects across populations, is relevant to whether evidence from an initial hedging program carries to other households and settings. ECO-08, Structural counterfactuals for macroeconomic regimes, concerns how outcomes change under different macroeconomic arrangements, which could inform stress evaluation. Neither the transport of effects nor the validity of structural counterfactuals is established merely by successful trading in these markets.

Synthesis from the supplied roster: ECO-03, A predictive and welfare-coherent theory of boundedly rational choice, overlaps with understanding household demand, comprehension and use of complicated long-horizon contracts. ECO-04, An interpersonally comparable, preference-respecting measure of welfare, concerns comparing welfare across people. ECO-06 can demonstrate reduced covered exposure and net benefits under explicit household-level measures without resolving either a general theory of choice or interpersonal welfare measurement.

Synthesis from the supplied roster: ECO-05, Approximately efficient voluntary provision of global public goods, addresses collective provision rather than insurance of household exposures, although both involve participation and institutional incentives. ECO-07, A verified, manipulable law of sustained productivity growth, concerns generating growth; national-income contracts would distribute exposure to growth outcomes without themselves establishing how to produce sustained growth.

Synthesis from the supplied roster: ECO-10, Liquidity and credit without run-prone debt, overlaps with the resilience of financing and intermediation supporting household hedges. ECO-06 instead targets which income and housing risks households can transfer. A successful hedge could still rely on fragile financing, while resilient credit institutions could exist without offering effective income or housing insurance.

Sovereign growth-indexed debt shares the idea of payments contingent on aggregate economic performance, but its immediate object is sovereign financing and debt risk. Household income insurance requires a further connection between contract payoffs and household exposures, access and costs. Similarly, exchange-rate models that explain currency disconnect concern a different explanatory problem; explaining currency behavior does not create national-income, occupational-income or housing claims. The referenced exchange-rate models were not identified in the supplied evidence.

The consumption-correlation and equity-home-bias puzzles overlap with the broader question of international risk sharing but remain distinct from ECO-06 and from one another. The former concerns the cross-country behavior of consumption relative to output; the latter concerns portfolio ownership. Their listing on the supplied Wikipedia page supports those distinctions, not a requirement that either puzzle disappear when household hedging improves.

unresolved_issues: The SSRN, BIS, IMF and CME sources have no retained artifacts. Their attributed arguments, dates, numerical findings and market observations remain unverified.
The IMF scenarios require their model assumptions, outcome definitions and premium treatment before their quantitative implications can be assessed.
The reported French bond episode and May 2026 Panageas paper lack a corresponding supplied source URL and reviewed text.
The empty bounded search record prevents an assessment of market completeness and freshness as of 1 November 2026.
The relative importance of moral hazard, adverse selection, financing constraints, startup liquidity and basis risk in each proposed contract family remains unresolved.
Concrete demonstration thresholds, welfare valuation methods and feasible data access must be specified before evaluating implementation.
No identified source supports the referenced exchange-rate models, so their relationship is retained only as a conceptual distinction.

brief.title: Household protection against shared economic losses
possible: Families could buy protection against falling incomes across their country or occupation, or falling house prices in their area. Contracts would pay when a shared index—a measure of income or prices—falls, with investors taking on the risk.

Households could get this protection directly or through pension and mortgage providers. It would cover shared economic losses, rather than every personal earnings loss or every home's change in value.
why: A family's future earnings can be hard to insure or borrow against. Affordable protection could help households withstand occupational decline and reduce pressure to keep savings tied to their own locality or economy.

sources.showed: This paper discusses proposed markets for shared economic risks and barriers to establishing them.
sources.cited_for: It supports the case for markets that transfer shared economic risks.
sources.not_established: A market proposal does not demonstrate affordable, lasting protection for households.

sources.showed: This working paper examines government bonds whose payments depend on economic growth and their effects on government debt risk.
sources.cited_for: It addresses a related use of contracts whose payments depend on economic growth.
sources.not_established: Reducing government debt risk does not demonstrate protection of household income.

sources.showed: This market page lists tradable contracts linked to metropolitan house-price measures and reports trading activity.
sources.cited_for: It provides an example of contracts tied to shared housing risk.
sources.not_established: Listing contracts does not establish sustained trading, household use or effective protection.

sources.showed: These discussion slides address constraints on using future earnings as security for borrowing.
sources.cited_for: They address households' difficulty financing protection against future income losses.
sources.not_established: A financing constraint does not establish how an affordable household protection system would work.

sources.showed: This overview describes limited ownership of foreign shares and the weaker connection between countries' consumption than between their output.
sources.quote: This puzzle concerns the observation that individuals and institutions in many countries only hold modest amounts of foreign equity, despite the ability for vast diversification of their portfolios in the global economy.
sources.cited_for: These international patterns are separate questions from whether households can protect themselves against shared losses.
sources.not_established: Describing these patterns does not demonstrate household income protection or require that successful protection eliminate them.

shown: Work has reached proposals for shared income markets and listed contracts tied to local house prices. Kocherlakota's review documents obstacles to insuring earnings and borrowing against them. These are components and motivations for household protection; lasting, affordable protection remains to be demonstrated.
missing: Households still need affordable contracts with willing buyers and sellers over long periods.
Protection must reduce actual household losses enough to outweigh all trading, financing and payment costs.
Contracts must remain usable during downturns, with households able to meet cash demands and receive promised payments.

milestones.label: Trading lasts for years with meaningful household participation
milestones.explanation: Trading would have to sustain buyers, sellers and meaningful household participation over a period of years, with criteria set beforehand. This would establish durability for the type of contract tested.

milestones.label: Household risk falls enough to outweigh full costs
milestones.explanation: An evaluation would have to meet a minimum risk reduction set beforehand, compared with households without protection, with benefits exceeding all costs. This would establish practical insurance value.

milestones.label: Protection works during downturns with reproducible results
milestones.explanation: Results would have to show that households retain protection, meet cash demands and receive payments during adverse shocks, with enough detail for independent assessment. This would establish performance when needed.

milestones.label: Repeated tests establish protection across groups and conditions
milestones.explanation: Repeated tests would have to demonstrate protection across household groups, occupations, places and economic conditions. This would establish how broadly the results apply.

uncertain: How closely can a shared measure track household losses without making payments depend on individual effort or reporting?
Which barriers matter most: financing, willing investors, reliable payments or a poor match between the index and household losses?
What minimum risk reduction and method of valuing benefits should count as success?

page.title: Macro markets for household income and house-price risk
page.definition: Households can hedge shared national-income, occupational-income and local house-price risk through long-term index-linked contracts, directly or through intermediaries. An index measures an aggregate exposure; a hedge offsets losses linked to it while leaving differences between the index and the household’s own losses.

goal.need: Corporate profits accounted for less than 10% of national income in the April 1999 New York Fed analysis, so equity markets supplied claims on only one part of income. The proposed markets extend hedging to shared national and occupational income shocks. Their benefit depends on the match between the index and household losses, financing requirements and trading costs.

statements.body: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
statements.quote: These markets would give investors an opportunity to trade long-term claims on the income of an entire country or region.
statements.context: The announcement of 24 March 1999 describes the researchers’ proposal; it does not announce a Federal Reserve implementation programme.

statements.body: MacroMarkets LLC chief economist Robert J. Shiller
statements.quote: We need to look ahead for institutional changes that would put household risk management on a more solid footing.
statements.context: From Shiller’s paper for the Sixth Annual BIS Conference, reproduced in a securities filing.

statements.quote: Manage the risk on your residential properties
statements.context: The stated purpose on CME’s residential real-estate futures page.

completion.title: Households obtain net insurance benefits from index markets in all three risk classes.
completion.criterion: For national-income, occupational-income and local house-price risk separately, households obtain index-linked hedges spanning their stated exposure period. Observed household outcomes show lower relevant income or wealth risk than an unhedged benchmark, with insurance benefits exceeding transaction, financing, margin, intermediation and settlement costs under an explicit valuation method. Contracts settle as promised through an adverse index movement, and replacement hedges remain available. The evaluation specifies its sample, horizon, risk measure and remaining mismatch between index payments and household losses.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no outside body’s completion test was identified.
completion.basis: Shiller’s proposals, the New York Fed analysis, BIS conference material, CFTC listing requirements, CME housing rules and the 2020 property-derivatives review were searched for a completion test. No end-to-end household-benefit criterion, common horizon, cost ceiling or participation minimum was found. This fallback requires the proposed insurance function to operate in each case; listing and index construction establish narrower results.

milestones.title: An index explains a nonzero share of household income or property-price variation.
milestones.criterion: An index explains a nonzero share of variation in household income or property values. Occupational: a 1995 working paper reports 50–74% of residual variance explained in 23,912 five-year log-income-change observations from U.S. data for 1968–1987. Housing: simulated ZIP-index protection covers 49.8% of losses in over 300,000 Los Angeles repeat sales during 1988–2001. These are historical fits, not realized insurance benefits. National: the 1999 study estimates GDP risk for 49 countries rather than household-level index fit.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; searches of the New York Fed, Cowles Foundation and Syracuse pilot sources found no common household-index validation threshold.

milestones.title: An index-linked futures contract is listed under CFTC product-listing requirements.
milestones.criterion: An index-linked futures contract is listed on a U.S. designated contract market through CFTC self-certification or product approval. This establishes regulated availability. Housing: CME housing futures launched on 22 May 2006; chapter 419 specifies ten metropolitan indices, cash settlement and a contract value of US$250 times the index. Corresponding national-income and occupational-income household hedging listings were not verified.
milestones.set_by: Commodity Futures Trading Commission, Listing Procedures, implementing 17 CFR 40.2 and 40.3; this is the U.S. exchange route.
milestones.threshold_quote: permits designated contract markets (DCMs) to list products for trading without prior CFTC approval by filing a written self-certification with the CFTC.

milestones.title: At least one household buys index protection for its own income or housing exposure.
milestones.criterion: At least one household, directly or through an intermediary, enters a binding index-linked contract covering its own exposure. Housing: the Syracuse programme reports its first homeowner purchase on 30 July 2002. Its published design offered protection for up to 30 years at a one-time fee of 1.5% of protected value. This working-paper report establishes a purchase, not a measured insurance benefit. National-income and occupational-income retail cohorts were not verified.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; searches for income-index insurance pilots and review of the Syracuse programme found no common retail-adoption threshold.

milestones.title: A household index hedge survives an adverse index movement and pays its contractual amount.
milestones.criterion: A household hedge remains in force through an adverse index movement and pays the beneficiary the amount due under its contract. Evidence concerns household beneficiaries rather than exchange settlement alone. CME chapter 419 specifies housing-futures settlement between clearing members and the clearing house, but does not identify household beneficiaries. No verified household payment cohort meeting this test was found for any of the three cases.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; searches of CFTC, CME and household-risk-sharing materials found no common household stress-performance test.

not_found: No accessible source established market-wide household participation or net hedge benefits across the three risk classes as of 14 November 2026.
The supplied CME quotation page exposed no numerical volume or open-interest data, preventing verification of the draft’s trading snapshot.
The supplied IMF page exposed bibliographic metadata but no working-paper text.
The ISDA page for its 2007 Property Index Derivative Definitions could not be opened.
